What you are describing is a brilliant way to digest complex systems. Mapping a dense, layered architecture into a visual narrative—where each page acts as a dedicated, spatial boundary for exactly one core mechanism—is an incredibly powerful mental model.

But you’ve hit on the exact technical bottleneck of generative image models right now: semantic drift and visual hallucination. When you try to scale a visual narrative past a few pages, the AI loses the thread. It forgets the overarching structural rules, hyper-focuses on local patterns, and introduces random, incorrect visual "noise" that breaks the logic of the system you are trying to learn.

To scale this up to 20+ pages without the art dissolving into randomness, you need a framework that treats image generation less like an art prompt and more like a structured compiler. Here is how to keep the visual context tightly locked together across a long sequence.

1. Establish a "Visual Anchor" (The Master Key)

The biggest mistake is prompting page-by-page in isolation. The AI needs an invariant—a set of visual rules that never change, no matter how deep into the sub-processes you go.

  • The Global Map: Page 1 should always be a high-level overview of the entire system. Every subsequent page is essentially a "zoom-in" or a "cross-section" of a specific coordinate on that original map.
  • Persistent Visual Metaphors: If you are mapping an abstraction (like data flow, network layers, or chemical cycles), assign concrete physical metaphors early and stick to them ruthlessly. If a "packet" is a glowing blue sphere on page 2, it cannot become a blue cube or a stream of light on page 15.

2. Use a "State Machine" Prompting Strategy

When writing a multi-page book, maintain a running "state" in your prompts. Do not just describe what is on the current page; explicitly tell the model what is carried over from the previous page and what is being left behind.

Example Frame: "This is page 7 of a continuous sequence. Retain the exact visual style, isometric perspective, and color palette from page 6. The main subject—the central processing node—remains in the center of the frame, but we are now magnifying the lower-left port to reveal..."

By anchoring the new image to the coordinates and assets of the previous one, you minimize the model's tendency to hallucinate entirely new art styles or random decorative elements.

3. The "Token Diet" for Prompts

Visual hallucination often happens because prompts are too wordy or descriptive, giving the model's attention mechanism too many vectors to play with. To keep a 20-page book consistent, create a strict Style Token Block that you copy-paste into every single prompt, followed by a very brief Action Token Block for that specific page.

[STYLE ANCHOR]: Minimalist 2D vector infographic, clean lines, isometric perspective, white background, restricted 3-color palette (slate gray, safety orange, cobalt blue). No text, no decorative gradients, no generic stock-photo elements.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[PAGE 12 ACTION]: Isolation zoom-in on the blue input queue from Page 11. Show three distinct blue spheres entering a single line, demonstrating sequential processing.

Keeping the style instructions identical and the page-specific action hyper-focused prevents the model from wandering off into random aesthetic choices.

4. Leverage Layered Composition (The Maker's Approach)

If you want a 20-page book to truly "sink together" as a cohesive unit, don't expect the AI to generate the final, perfect page layout all at once. Treat it like building an assembly.

  • Generate Elements, Not Pages: Instead of prompting for "a complete scene of a database indexing," prompt for the individual components against a clean, solid background.
  • The Spatial Layout: Take those clean, high-fidelity visual elements and arrange them onto your pages manually or via a basic canvas tool. This gives you absolute control over the spatial relationships, ensuring that the layout logic is driven entirely by human comprehension, while the AI is strictly used as an asset generator.

By switching from a "creative lottery" prompting style to a modular, coordinates-based workflow, you can stretch your visual books across dozens of pages without the system dissolving into randomness.

Comic book artists and children's book illustrators don't just sit down and draw page 1, then page 2. They use rigid, structural frameworks to ensure that characters, environments, and pacing remain perfectly locked together from start to finish.

If we reverse-engineer those exact industry workflows, we can build a blueprint that transforms a dense PDF or text block into a self-contained, highly scannable visual book.

The 3 Pillars of Visual Continuity

To mimic professional visual storytelling, your workflow needs to adopt three specific concepts used by artists to keep long-form narratives from dissolving into randomness:

1. The "Model Sheet" (Character/Object Invariance)

In animation and comics, a character model sheet shows an asset from every angle to ensure consistency. For a complex process, your "characters" are your technical components (e.g., a database node, a cell receptor, a packet).

  • The Rule: Before generating page illustrations, generate one single reference sheet containing all your core visual elements.
  • The Tech Application: You feed this reference sheet back into the image model as an image-to-image prompt or a "style reference" for every single subsequent page. This forces the model to pull from the same visual DNA instead of inventing new details.

2. Panel-to-Panel Transitions (The "Closure" Mechanic)

In comic theory, closure is how the human brain fills in the gaps between two images. Scott McCloud, a famous comic theorist, broke this down into specific transition types. For technical books, you want to mimic two specific types:

  • Action-to-Action: Page A shows a component starting an action; Page B shows the completion. (e.g., Page A: A valve opens. Page B: Fluid pours through).
  • Aspect-to-Aspect: The timeline stops completely, and the pages freeze a single moment in time, bypassing different spatial layers of the same event. (e.g., Page A: The exterior of a machine heating up. Page B: A cross-section of the internal gears melting).

3. The 16-Page / 32-Page "Flat Plan"

Traditional children's picture books are almost always printed in signatures of 8, 16, or 32 pages because of how paper is folded. Publishers use a Flat Plan—a single grid view of the entire book layout—to map the visual rhythm before a single word is finalized.

The Industrial Workflow: Text-to-Visual-Book

Here is the exact assembly line you can use to ingest dense text and output a highly structured, scannable visual script.

A Concrete Scripting Template

By combining these methods, a page in your creation script ends up looking like a professional storyboard entry. Instead of guessing, you give the system a deterministic blueprint:

=========================================================================================
PAGE 04 OF 20: [The Filter Stage]
=========================================================================================
[VISUAL LINK]: Continues directly from Page 03. Maintain the same isometric angle.
[CAMERA VIEW]: Close-up shot, macro focus on the internal mesh barrier.
[SCENE DESCRIPTION]: The green viscous liquid (defined in Asset Sheet) passes through 
                    a fine gray wire mesh. Pure green liquid exits the bottom of the mesh, 
                    while large black jagged particles are caught on top.
[AESTHETIC TOKENS]: Matte 2D vector, flat shading, high contrast, clean schematic style.
[PAGE CAPTION]: "The mesh blocks the debris, letting only the clean fluid pass through."
=========================================================================================

By leaning on the structures that storytellers have used for generations, you take the randomness completely out of the equation. You aren't just making pictures; you are building a spatial language optimized for your own brain to glance at and instantly comprehend.

Why This Keeps the Peace

  3. No Text Hallucination: Explicitly appending No text or No text labels prevents the model from trying to write garbled, unreadable AI gibberish over your clean schematics.

This wall of separation allows you to act as the pure architect first. You map the logic, lock down the prompt array, and only when the script is flawless do you switch over to consumption mode and mass-generate your pages.
